bibliography.abstract: Trail planning and development continue to grow in support of the increased demand for pedestrian and bicycle mobility throughout the country. With this growth in trail facilities, understanding how transportation justice, specifically trail modal access, can be measured and evaluated is valuable. The term trail deserts is presented in this study as a way to describe geographic areas where residents have little to no opportunities for trail mobility. This study focuses on the development of a seven-step method using GIS to define trail access and desert areas based on modal access (pedestrian, bicycle, and vehicular) as well as to understand relationships related to demographic and land use factors. This method is unique as it introduces and defines the term trail deserts. Also, a modal accessibility scale (high, medium, and low) is developed using a buffer approach (pedestrian and bicycle) and roadway network analysis approach (vehicular) to determine trail access. This approach is advantageous as it reflects the variations in modal accessibility between both nonvehicular and vehicular access to trail facilities. A case study on Pennsylvania is conducted and the method is presented so that transportation planning organizations (such as Metropolitan Planning Organizations and DOT agencies) can apply the process to their own jurisdictions to improve trail improvement and prioritization processes.

bibliography.title: Methodology for Identifying Trail Deserts: Exploring Modal Access to Trails through Demographic and Land Use Factors

publication_status.journal: Journal of Urban Planning and Development

en.caveats: While the methodology is designed for broad application by planning organizations, its performance and classification thresholds are demonstrated only within the single state context of Pennsylvania.
en.what: This study establishes a seven-step GIS-based methodology to define and map 'trail deserts' where residents lack pedestrian, bicycle, or vehicular access to trail networks. Using a buffer approach for non-vehicular modes and roadway network analysis for vehicular access, the method classifies accessibility into high, medium, and low tiers, and evaluates these patterns against demographic and land use factors across a statewide case study of Pennsylvania.
en.why: It introduces a standardized, multi-modal definition of trail deserts, allowing transportation planning agencies to identify specific geographic gaps in non-motorized infrastructure and prioritize trail investments based on equity and modal access.
